other_up.note:
Two standard steps. First, for any decision tree $T$ computing $f$,
$\mathrm{Inf}_i(f) \le \Pr_x[T \text{ queries } i]$ -- if $f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})$
and $T$ never queried $i$, then $x$ and $x^{\oplus i}$ follow the same path
and get the same answer. Summing over $i$ gives
$\mathrm{I}(f) \le \mathbb{E}_x[\#\text{queries}]$. Second, in a tree where
no coordinate is queried twice a leaf at depth $d_\ell$ is reached with
probability exactly $2^{-d_\ell}$, so
$\mathbb{E}_x[\#\text{queries}] = \sum_\ell p_\ell \log_2(1/p_\ell)$ is the
entropy of a distribution on $\mathrm{DTsize}(f)$ outcomes, hence at most
$\log_2 \mathrm{DTsize}(f)$.

other_lo.note: Attained exactly: the minimal tree for $\oplus_n$ is the full binary tree on $2^n$ leaves and every coordinate is fully influential.

  • \(\mathrm{I}(f) \le \log_2 \mathrm{DTsize}(f)\)
    putative ODonnell14
    Two standard steps. First, for any decision tree $T$ computing $f$, $\mathrm{Inf}_i(f) \le \Pr_x[T \text{ queries } i]$ -- if $f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})$ and $T$ never queried $i$, then $x$ and $x^{\oplus i}$ follow the same path and get the same answer. Summing over $i$ gives $\mathrm{I}(f) \le \mathbb{E}_x[\#\text{queries}]$. Second, in a tree where no coordinate is queried twice a leaf at depth $d_\ell$ is reached with probability exactly $2^{-d_\ell}$, so $\mathbb{E}_x[\#\text{queries}] = \sum_\ell p_\ell \log_2(1/p_\ell)$ is the entropy of a distribution on $\mathrm{DTsize}(f)$ outcomes, hence at most $\log_2 \mathrm{DTsize}(f)$.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{I}(\oplus_n) = n = \log_2 \mathrm{DTsize}(\oplus_n)\)
    witness: \(\oplus_n\)
    Attained exactly: the minimal tree for $\oplus_n$ is the full binary tree on $2^n$ leaves and every coordinate is fully influential.

Strictly stronger than $\mathrm{I}(f)\le\mathrm{D}(f)$, since $\log_2\mathrm{DTsize}\le\mathrm{D}$: a wide shallow tree bounds the influence by its size, not its depth. The first step above is the same observation that drives the OSSS inequality.

see also: \(\mathrm{I}(f)\), \(\mathrm{DTsize}(f)\), \(\mathrm{D}(f)\), \(\mathrm{MaxInf}(f)\), \(\oplus_n\) data/relations/05-fourier.yaml

  • \(\mathrm{I}(f) \le \mathrm{s}(f)\)
    witness: \(\oplus_n\) ODonnell14
    Total influence is the average number of sensitive coordinates, sensitivity the maximum. Equality for $\mathrm{PARITY}_n$ (both $=n$).

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{I}(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = n\)
    witness: \(\oplus_n\)
    Every coordinate is sensitive at every input, so the average and the maximum coincide: the inequality is attained with nothing to spare.
  • \(\mathrm{I}(f) \text{ can be exponentially smaller than } \mathrm{s}(f)\)
    witness: \(\mathrm{AND}_n\)
    $\mathrm{I}(\wedge_n) = n\,2^{-(n-1)}$ while $\mathrm{s}(\wedge_n)=n$. Influence is an average-case measure, so it is not comparable to the worst-case zoo in the usual way.

Influence-type measures sit slightly outside the main lattice: they lower bound average-case rather than worst-case complexity. The useful direction is always $\mathrm{I}(f) \le (\text{worst-case measure})$.

see also: \(\mathrm{I}(f)\), \(\mathrm{s}(f)\), \(\mathrm{MaxInf}(f)\), \(\mathrm{D}(f)\) data/relations/05-fourier.yaml

Proved from degree statistics of certain subgraphs of the hypercube, and it recovers most earlier noisy lower bounds up to constants. It settles Open Problem 2 of [Gu25noisy], which had the statement only at the top of the range ($\mathrm{I}(f) = \Omega(n)$, giving $\Theta(n\log n)$).

  • \(\mathrm{I}(f)\log \mathrm{I}(f) = O\big(\mathrm{N}_p(f)\big),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \mathrm{I}(f) = O\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{N}_p(f)}{\log \mathrm{N}_p(f)}\right)\)
    GLX26noisy Gu25noisy
    Equivalently $\mathrm{N}_p(f) = \Omega(\mathrm{I}(f)\log \mathrm{I}(f))$ for every total Boolean $f$ -- the first general lower bound on $\mathrm{N}_p$ beyond $\mathrm{N}_p \ge \Omega(\mathrm{R})$. Proved from degree statistics of certain subgraphs of the hypercube, and it recovers most earlier noisy lower bounds up to constants. It settles Open Problem 2 of [Gu25noisy], which had the statement only at the top of the range ($\mathrm{I}(f) = \Omega(n)$, giving $\Theta(n\log n)$).

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{I}(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = n,\quad \mathrm{N}_p(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = \Theta(n\log n)\)
    witness: \(\oplus_n\) FRPU94 EvansPippenger98
    So the bound is tight: the $\log$ cannot be dropped from $\mathrm{I}\log \mathrm{I} = O(\mathrm{N}_p)$.

Read the arrow in the zoo's direction and this is a bound on influence: a function with a lot of influence cannot be computed with few noisy queries. Read it backwards and it is a lower bound on $\mathrm{N}_p$. It therefore sits in this cell and not in $\mathrm{N}_p \to \mathrm{I}$, where the entry is a separation (OR has $\mathrm{I} = n2^{1-n}$ but $\mathrm{N}_p = \Theta(n)$) and where no upper bound exists at all: no function of $\mathrm{I}$ bounds $\mathrm{N}_p$. Both statements say "$\mathrm{N}_p$ is large compared to $\mathrm{I}$" and neither constrains the other.

Stated for total Boolean $f$, where $\mathrm{I}(f)=\sum_S |S|\hat f(S)^2$ is the usual total influence; the noisy model itself is happy with partial functions and relations, but influence is not defined off a total domain without choosing what happens outside the promise.

see also: \(\mathrm{I}(f)\), \(\mathrm{N}_{p}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\oplus_n\), \(\mathrm{OR}_n\), Two different noisy query models, \(\mathrm{I}^{1}(f)\) data/relations/04-composition.yaml
